Family a.298.1.1 groups these domains because they share the same modular repeat architecture, not because they have similar total length. TAL effectors (from Xanthomonas) have a central array of tandem repeats, each about 33-35 residues. Each repeat folds as a helix-turn-helix unit, and the repeats stack into a right-handed superhelix. The number of repeats varies widely in natural TAL effectors (roughly 1.5 to 34), so a SCOPe domain covering the array can range from a few repeats to the whole array plus flanking regions. The three named domains (d2kq5a_, d3v6pa_, d4cj9a_, all chain A of PDB entries 2kq5, 3v6p and 4cj9) differ in length because they contain different numbers of repeats and different flanking segments. They should not be read as different folds or as evidence against family membership.

Family-level membership rests on the conserved repeat-unit fold, which is a structural relationship. Repeats within one array are highly similar, but they are not identical: the repeat-variable diresidue (RVD) positions in the second helix differ, and those residues determine DNA base preference. Sharing the family therefore says nothing about DNA-binding specificity. Two TAL domains in the same family can bind different DNA sequences, and specificity should not be transferred from one domain to another without experimental evidence such as the RVD-to-base code or binding assays.

Limits: I cannot verify the source structures, exact SCOPe boundaries, or the a.298.1.1 assignment from pretrained knowledge alone in this blind setting, so I am relying on the classification given in the prompt. SCOPe domain boundaries for repeat proteins are chosen by curators and can differ from the full biological array, so length comparisons between domains depend on those choices. Class a is all-alpha, which fits the helical repeats, but I am not certain of the fold name for a.298 from memory. Fold and family membership do not imply the same function, and any functional claim about a specific domain would need direct experimental or structural evidence for that domain.
